abstract.t: This document specifies an algorithm with two input variants for comparing revisions of a YANG schema to determine the scope of changes and produce a list of the changes between the revisions. The output of the algorithm can be used to help select an appropriate YANG semantic version number for a new YANG Module revision. It also specifies a YANG module for YANG-structured output of these algorithms, that can be easily consumed in a machine-readable way.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: This document defines a common algorithm for comparing two revisions of a YANG schema. As input, there can be two types of YANG schema representations: single locally resolved YANG modules or fully resolved set of YANG modules (on-the-wire schema). The algorithm output for each of these representations serves a different purpose. It can help YANG authors with assigning the correct semantic version of a module based on or tools processing YANG instance data can use it to learn about the exact data changes, respectively.

The algorithm operates in a straightforward way traversing all the statements and their substatements in both the old and new module representations collecting identified changes. These are then reported in a concise output with information about the overall backwards compatibility between the two modules. Exact output format is out of scope for this document but Appendix A includes an example of a YANG module whose YANG data can represent all the possible changes and so a complete output of this algorithm.

Every change is classified as editorial, backwards-compatible, or non-backwards-compatible. This conformance is decided based on rules found in other documents, specifically , , and . For older YANG 1.0 modules, the rules in apply instead.

section.name: Terminology and Conventions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

This document makes use of the following terminology introduced in the YANG 1.1 Data Modeling Language :
module schema node data node data definition statement

In addition, this document uses the following terminology:
locally resolved module: A parsed YANG module with all its submodules and local references resolved. fully resolved schema: A locally resolved module with all the imported references resolved as well and with non data definition statements removed.

section.name: Schema representations
section.t: The YANG language defines several statements that act as syntactic abstraction and need to be processed before a YANG module can be used for handling YANG instance data. For example, a “uses” statement is replaced by all the substatements of a referenced “grouping” statement or a “typedef” statement can be linked to other “type” statements. The referenced statements can be local (defined in the same module, or included submodule) but also foreign (defined in another imported module).

section.name: Locally resolved module (single module)
section.t: This representation of a YANG module includes all submodules of the main module but resolves only statements that reference other statements found in the same module. No references to imported modules (that are using an imported prefix) are resolved.
For example, any changes of a referenced “typedef” or “grouping” defined in an imported module would not affect the locally resolved module and are out of scope for this representation.
All the rules for classifying individual statement changes mentioned in apply to this module representation.

section.name: Deviation
section.t: Regardless of whether the “deviation” target node is local in the same module or in an imported module, it is never resolved and applied. Instead, the “deviation” statement with all its substatements is kept in the locally resolved module so that it can be considered in the schema comparison algorithm.

section.name: Refine
section.t: The “refine” statement is processed differently based on whether the affected “grouping” is defined in an imported module or the local YANG module. In the former case, when the relevant grouping is imported, the “refine” is not resolved and kept in the module. And then examined in the comparison algorithm, similarly to the “deviation” statement.

However, all the “refine” statements targeting a local “grouping” are applied on the nodes of the grouping when the “uses” is resolved. After processing the “refine” statements with all its substatements, they are effectively removed from the locally resolved module to avoid reporting changes of any “refine” statements twice.

section.name: Augment
section.t: All the “augment” statements are processed similarly to “refine” statements. Meaning that augments of imported groupings are not resolved and compared directly while augments of local groupings are applied and then removed from the module.

section.name: Fully resolved schema (set of modules)
section.t: The fully resolved schema representation consists of one or more YANG modules. Each of these is fully resolved according to the rules of the YANG language meaning that every referenced statement, including to other imported modules, is resolved, unlike locally resolved modules. The result is one large tree with schema nodes of all the YANG modules. The comparison algorithm MAY then choose to compare top-level schema node subtrees belonging only to a single YANG module.

Next, all the statements used only for syntactic abstraction that do not affect YANG instance data are removed. Note that the “description” or “units” statements are kept because they may influence the data. Also, “error-app-tag” and “error-message” statements remain in the fully resolved schema for applications to learn that the generated error information has changed.
The steps taken when fully resolving a module include:

ul.li: All submodules of a single module are merged to create one large YANG module.
"Import" statements are resolved by finding the referenced YANG modules and making their contents available.

"Uses" statements are replaced by the referenced "groupings" and the YANG nodes they define.
Any “when” statement of the “uses” is moved down to all the direct descendant schema nodes of the “grouping”.
Types referencing any "typedef" statements are replaced with the actual type details.

Augments are resolved by placing the included YANG nodes in their targets.
Any “when” statement of the “augment” is moved down to all the direct descendant schema nodes of the “augment”.
"Deviation" and "refine" statements are applied by changing the appropriate schema nodes.
All the "if-feature" statements are evaluated based on the enabled "features" of implemented YANG modules and the disabled schema nodes are removed.
All the extension-instances have a matching “extension” defintion.

section.t: After the resolution, the following statements are completely removed with their substatements:
Also, these schema nodes are removed but replaced with their schema node substatements:

The term “schema” was chosen instead of “module” on purpose because when statements are imported from external modules, the resulting schema then includes statements from several YANG modules. But the fully resolved schema representation of a module always includes only the top-level schema node trees of that module.
Only a subset of the module update rules in apply for the fully resolved schema. Specifically, the rules for removed statements cannot be applied but other present statements are processed normally.

How the concrete set of YANG modules of a fully resolved schema is described is out of scope of this document. But suitable existing structures include YANG data of “ietf-yang-library” from or “ietf-yang-package-instance” in .

section.name: Choosing a schema representation
section.t: Selecting a suitable schema representation for the comparison algorithm depends on the desired purpose. But for a complete set of changes, both the representations should be compared and their output merged to get the combined output of the two comparisons.

YANG module authors will primarily be interested in the locally resolved module representation. Using it for the comparison algorithm will yield all the changes that occurred in the specific YANG module only while ignoring any possible changes in imported modules. This information can then directly be used to decide the correct semantic version of the new revision of this module. The rules for selecting versions are defined in .

Any YANG-based application handling YANG instance data always uses the fully resolved schema representation. So, when running the schema comparison algorithm with the intent of learning the changes in the corresponding valid YANG instance data of the module, this representation should be used. With some additional information, the output of this comparison can then also be used to transform valid data of the old schema revision to data valid for the new schema revision. All these tools and applications are typically clients or servers of YANG-driven protocols, e.g. NETCONF, RESTCONF, or gRPC.

section.name: Examples
section.t: To illustrate the different output of the comparison algorithm each schema representation can generate for the same YANG module changes, following are a few examples.

When a “typedef” or “grouping” name changes, the algorithm for locally resolved module will detect the change and report it as non-backwards-compatible. This is useful especially when importing such a module to learn that any references to the original statements will no longer be valid. However, if using the fully resolved schema, this difference will not be detected at all since it does not affect YANG instance data corresponding to this module.

Another specific use-case is when a module with “uses” that referenced an external “grouping” replaces that “uses” node directly with schema nodes in the “grouping” effectively resolving the “uses” similarly to a YANG module parser. Such a change is non-backwards-compatible based on the YANG 1.1 updating rules and reported that way when using a locally resolved module. But the fully resolved schemas will be completely the same before and after the change so the comparison algorithm will not generate any changes and report full compatibility of the old and the new modules with their instance data.

section.name: Comparison algorithm
section.t: This algorithm is defined for individual locally resolved modules and fully resolved schemas. All the statements are compared with their content, recursively, in the old revision and the new revision of the module or schema. Depth-first search order for the statement traversal SHOULD be used.

The non data definition statements are considered modified when their content is changed or any of their substatements are changed. If a statement is present in the old revision and missing in the new revision, it is considered removed. Conversely, if missing in the old revision but present in the new revision, it is considered added.

Data definition statements are compared similarly except that a change in a descendant data definition statement is not considered a change of the parent data definition statement but a separate change instead.
Only statements with any changes are reported and included in the comparison algorithm output.

section.name: Module identification
section.t: When generating the comparison output of two modules, unique identification of these modules SHOULD be included. For both the old and the new revision of the base module, its name, revision, list of submodules, and a leaf-list of enabled features is included. For the fully resolved schema, the same information is also reported for all the imported YANG modules, recursively. This ensures that if any other output is produced with a different set of changes for two fully resolved schemas, their identification information must also differ.

section.name: Change conformance
section.t:
Every change is classified as editorial, backwards-compatible, or non-backwards-compatible. The classification is based on Section 11 of which mentions most of the possible changes between two revisions of a YANG 1.1 module and Section 3.1 of
adds more details about the exact conformance of statements with various "status" statement values. Finally,
defines what classifies as an editorial change.
General non-normative explanation of change conformance classification can be found in .

section.name: Deviations, Refines, and Augments
section.t: All the statement change conformance follows the general rules above if these statements are present in the schema representation, see . But this clarification is added to make certain that the rules are interpreted correctly.

Since “deviation” and “refine” statements are not among the allowed statements that can be changed when updating a module in Section 11 of , any non-editorial change of these statements or their substatements is treated as non-backwards-compatible.
But since “augment” statements can only add schema nodes, these can be processed and compared normally.

So, for example, even if removing the “mandatory” statement is considered backwards-compatible, a new “deviation” removing the “mandatory” statement from its target node is considered a non-backwards-compatible change. Similarly a “refine” of the “description” of a node is classified as non-backward-compatible change. However, a change in the “description” of a “deviation” statement is treated as a standard “description” change because it describes the “deviation” statement itself and does not affect the deviation target node.

section.name: Conformance extensions
section.t: There are cases when it may be impossible for tooling to accurately determine the conformance of a change but a default conformance is always assumed for every statement. The affected ambiguous statements with their default conformances are:

Normally, any modification of these statements is reported with the default change conformance. However, if the author of the new revision of a YANG module determines that the change of one of the aforementioned statements has a different conformance based on the compatibility rules for the specific statement, they can decide to use the special extension instances to signify this fact. These are:

They determine the conformance of the change of the marked statement to be editorial, backwards-compatible, or non-backwards-compatible, respectively. The argument is a semantic version of the YANG module revision that introduced the specific change and these extension instances are sticky, meaning they remain in the module even in its later revisions. Also, a YANG statement can have multiple conformance extension statements. For example, when a pattern changes in multiple versions of a module, each change can be marked with an extension to explicitly state the conformance of the change.

section.name: Algorithm variants support
section.t: Tools implementing schema comparison SHOULD support comparing locally resolved modules, fully resolved schemas, and both representations together. In case the comparison generates YANG data for the "ietf-yang-schema-comparison-output" YANG module, simple XPath filters can be used to select any subset of changes.

Data definition statements are present in both the locally resolved module and fully resolved schema. So if both representations are compared normally, there would be duplicate changes reported in the algorithm output. These duplicate changes MUST be avoided and filtered out.

section.name: Schema Comparison YANG Module
section.t: YANG module with extensions for fine-tuning the classification of differences between two revisions of YANG schemas.

section.name: Contributors
section.t: This document grew out of the YANG module versioning design team that was formed after IETF 101. The following individuals are (or have been) members of the design team and have contributed on the YANG versioning project:
The idea of a tooling-based comparison of YANG module revisions was first described in . This document builds on those initial ideas.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: This section is modeled after the template described in Section 3.7.1 of .

The YANG modules specified in this document define extensions ("ietf-yang-schema-comparison") and a schema for data ("ietf-yang-schema-comparison-output") that are designed to be used by offline tooling to generate output describing the differences between two supplied YANG modules.

The YANG module specified in this document MAY be accessed via network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF . The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is Secure Shell (SSH) . The lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is TLS .

The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) provides the means to restrict access for particular NETCONF or RESTCONF users to a preconfigured subset of all available NETCONF or RESTCONF protocol operations and content.
When the module is used by offline tooling, there are no security considerations, since the user has full access to all YANG modules being used.

The "schema-comparison" structure defined in the "ietf-yang-schema-comparison-output" module contains all the groupings reflecting the changes between YANG modules. If instances of this structure are generated or published by online tooling, care needs to be taken so that information about non-public YANG modules is not inadvertently disclosed.
Since the module does not define any RPCs, actions, or notifications, the security considerations for such statements are not provided here.

section.name: Schema Comparison Algorithm Output YANG Module
section.t: This YANG module defines the specific output of the schema comparison algorithm, supporting comparison of the locally resolved module, fully resolved schema, or both. The "ietf-yang-schema-comparison-output" YANG module imports definitions from the "ietf-yang-types" module defined in , the "ietf-yang-library" module defined in , and the "ietf-yang-structure-ext" module defined in .

Generating schema comparison data in the form of YANG instance data compliant with this YANG module is optional but makes it easier for further automatic processing by tools and also allows for simple filtering of the data.

Non data definition statements are uniquely identified with their YANG identifier and data definition statements with their absolute schema node-ids. For every change, the changed statement and the parent of the changed statement are included. While redundant in many cases, it allows the algorithm to uniquely report changes in nested statements, e.g. an extension instance change in the type of a leaf statement. Also, all the unchanged substatements with their value or content are included for every changed statement, for both the older and the newer revision of the YANG module, if applicable. This ensures that the output includes all the possibly required information without relying on learning it from the YANG modules themselves.

section.name: Change Conformance Principles
section.t: This appendix clarifies the general principles based on which statement changes are categorized. They are not meant to replace any specification but rather help with understanding it.

section.name: Editorial change
section.t: An editorial change does not affect valid YANG data of the semantics of the YANG module in any way. That is, it does not make the valid data value space smaller or larger and it must remain exactly the same as in the module revision without the change. Also, for a change to be editorial, it must not affect any YANG module importing the changed YANG module.

In addition to obvious editorial changes such as fixing a typo in a "description", changing the local "prefix" of the module is also categorized as editorial because it does not affect importing modules. Or, replacing a "uses" statement directly with the nodes in the referenced "grouping" without any other changes.

section.name: Backwards-compatible change
section.t: For a change to be backwards-compatible, it has to expand the value space of valid YANG data. That is, all the valid YANG data nodes and values before the change must remain valid but additional nodes or values can also become valid after the change. Also, backwards-compatible changes may influence importing modules but must not cause them to become invalid. In other words, they may expose new statements whose removal would then be considered a non-backwards-compatible change but generally must not change the already exposed statements.
For some examples, the majority of possible backwards-compatible changes are specifically mentioned directly in Section 11 of .

section.name: Non-backwards-compatible change
section.t: If a change is not editorial nor backwards-compatible, it is then categorized as non-backwards-compatible. Such changes shrink the value space of valid YANG data, causing some previously valid nodes or values to no longer be valid. Also, any change that may cause an importing module to become invalid according to the YANG specification must be non-backwards-compatible.

Examples of less common or less obvious compatibility-breaking changes are changing the "yang-version" of a YANG module or expanding the size of a "type". The former change may break importing modules because of specific rules defined for the "import" statement and the target module's YANG version. Changing a "type" of a leaf from "uint32" to "uint64" may seem to fit the definition of a backwards-compatible change, but it may not be so for some data encodings that use a fixed binary data chunk (which would grow in size) or even a text format that may use a different encoding for the two types. Specifically, the JSON YANG data format encodes a "uint32" value as a JSON number but a "uint64" as a JSON string.

section.name: Comparison Examples
section.t: This section provides several examples of the output from the comparison algorithm defined in this document to illustrate its behavior on actual YANG modules. The example YANG modules are missing “description” or “reference” statements for better readability. Changes are represented as JSON encoded YANG instance data following the “ietf-yang-schema-comparison-output” module definition in for the output.

section.title: New Leaves Module
section.t: In this example, two new leaves are added to the module.

In the generated output, there are changes in both locally resolved module and fully resolved schema. The changes are backward-compatible because the new nodes are added without affecting the order of the existing schema nodes.

section.title: Relaxed Length Module
section.t: An example module comparison in which a typedef length restriction is relaxed and a new leaf is added.

The generated diff includes both locally resolved and fully resolved changes. In the local comparison, the specific range change is reported as backward-compatible because the restriction was relaxed. In the fully resolved node comparison, the exact same change is reported because the leaf uses the same typedef, whose change also affects the leaf. The newly added leaf is also reported and marked as backward-compatible.
